subject: Geography
statusNote: Paper structure (three papers, durations, marks including SPaG, weightings, sections and question rules), every section and key idea of the subject content, the required case studies and examples, AO weightings and the fieldwork rules were read from AQA's specification PDF through a summarising reader, not as raw text, so status is Provisional. The options taught and the case studies follow the school's ISS1 Curriculum Booklet 2026-27.

sources.title: Tarbiyyah Secondary School for Boys: Curriculum Overview 2026-27 (booklet, ISS1 SharePoint; staff only)

assessment.title: Living with the physical environment
assessment.content: 3.1.1 natural hazards, 3.1.2 the living world, 3.1.3 physical landscapes in the UK, 3.4 skills. 3 of the marks are for SPaG.
assessment.format: Section A all questions (33); Section B all questions (25); Section C any two of questions 3, 4 and 5 (30). Multiple choice, short answer, levels of response, extended prose.

assessment.title: Challenges in the human environment
assessment.content: 3.2.1 urban issues, 3.2.2 the changing economic world, 3.2.3 resource management, 3.4 skills. 3 of the marks are for SPaG.
assessment.format: Section A all questions (33); Section B all questions (30); Section C question 3 and one of 4, 5 or 6 (25).

assessment.title: Geographical applications
assessment.content: 3.3.1 issue evaluation (pre-release resources booklet 12 weeks before the exam), 3.3.2 fieldwork, 3.4 skills. 6 of the marks are for SPaG.
assessment.format: Section A all questions (37); Section B all questions (39).

nonExam: No coursework, but two fieldwork enquiries using primary data are required, in contrasting environments, on at least two occasions outside the classroom and school grounds, one on physical-human interaction. The centre must send AQA a signed Head of Centre statement; Paper 3 Section B asks about the pupil's own enquiries.

aos.desc: Knowledge of locations, places, processes, environments and scales.
Understanding of concepts and how places, environments and processes interrelate.
Apply knowledge to interpret, analyse and evaluate information and issues and make judgements.
Select, adapt and use skills and techniques to investigate questions and communicate findings.

units.title: Geographical skills, taught throughout
points: Cartographic skills: atlas and Ordnance Survey maps, maps with photographs.
Graphical skills: construct, choose and interpret graphs, charts and maps.
Numerical and statistical skills: scale, ratio, averages, spread, percentage change and trends.
Use qualitative and quantitative data, including GIS and satellite images.
Build an enquiry and an evidenced argument.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Natural hazards and tectonic hazards
points: Natural hazards pose major risks to people and property; types and factors affecting risk.
Earthquakes and volcanoes come from processes at plate margins; their global pattern.
Effects of and responses to a tectonic hazard differ between areas of contrasting wealth (two named examples).
Monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the effects; why people live in hazard zones.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Weather hazards: global circulation, tropical storms (Cyclone Idai) and UK weather hazards (Somerset floods, 2014)
points: Global atmospheric circulation shapes patterns of weather and climate.
Tropical storms form under particular physical conditions; distribution, structure and links to climate change.
Primary and secondary effects of, and responses to, a named tropical storm (school example: Cyclone Idai).
UK weather hazards and a recent extreme event (school example: Somerset Levels floods, 2014).
Evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Climate change
points: Evidence for climate change from the Quaternary period to the present.
Natural and human factors causing climate change, and its effects on people and the environment.
Managing climate change: mitigation and adaptation.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: The living world: ecosystems
points: Ecosystems involve interaction between biotic and abiotic parts at a range of scales.
A small-scale UK ecosystem: food webs, nutrient cycling and the effect of change.
An overview of the distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems.
units.foundingYear: Not taught in 2027 (TGA opens in January): taught from Autumn 2027, as in the school's booklet.

units.title: Tropical rainforests (case study: deforestation in Malaysia)
points: Distinctive characteristics of tropical rainforests: climate, soils, plants, animals and biodiversity.
Causes and economic and environmental impacts of deforestation (school case study: Malaysia).
Value of rainforests and strategies for sustainable management.

units.title: Hot deserts (school option; cold environments not taught)
points: Distinctive characteristics of hot deserts and how plants and animals adapt.
Opportunities and challenges of developing a hot desert (case study).
Desertification on desert fringes: causes and strategies to reduce it.

units.title: UK physical landscapes
points: The UK's diverse landscapes: location of upland and lowland areas and main river systems.
How geology and past processes created upland and lowland landscapes.

units.title: Coastal landscapes in the UK (examples: Swanage and Lyme Regis)
points: Waves, weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition shape the coast.
Erosional and depositional landforms on a named UK coastline (school example: Swanage).
Hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat; a UK coastal management scheme (school example: Lyme Regis).

units.title: River landscapes in the UK (River Tees; flood management at Banbury)
points: Long and cross profiles change downstream through erosion, transport and deposition.
Erosional and depositional landforms in a named UK river valley (school example: the River Tees).
Flood risk, hydrographs and hard and soft flood management; a UK scheme (school example: Banbury, taught in Summer).

units.title: Issue evaluation (pre-release resources)
points: A synoptic, critical-thinking section on a contemporary issue drawn from 3.1 and 3.2.
Use the pre-release resources booklet issued 12 weeks before the exam.
Weigh stakeholders' views and alternatives; justify a decision.

units.title: Fieldwork: two enquiries
points: Two enquiries with primary data in contrasting environments, one physical-human.
Enquiry stages: question, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusion and evaluation.
Questions on unfamiliar fieldwork materials and on the pupil's own enquiries.
units.resources: The booklet does not place fieldwork; placed in Year 10 Summer 2 with the issue evaluation preparation. Private candidates need a centre that can sign the Head of Centre fieldwork statement: confirm before entry.

units.title: Urban issues and challenges (case studies: Rio de Janeiro and Bristol)
points: Global urbanisation trends, causes and megacities.
Urban growth in an LIC or NEE city (school case study: Rio de Janeiro), with an urban planning example.
Opportunities and challenges in a major UK city (school case study: Bristol), with a regeneration project.
Urban sustainability: resources, green space and transport.
units.foundingYear: Founding-year Year 11 joins in January: covered in the Spring 1 catch-up and revision, as far as the cohort needs (to confirm with each pupil's prior school).

units.title: The changing economic world (case study: Nigeria; the changing UK economy)
points: Measuring development, causes of uneven development and the demographic transition model.
Strategies to close the development gap, including a tourism example in an LIC or NEE.
Rapid development in an LIC or NEE (school case study: Nigeria, a newly emerging economy), taught in Spring.
Changes in the UK economy: deindustrialisation, services, regional differences and the UK's place in the world.
units.foundingYear: Founding-year Year 11 joins in January: covered in the Spring 1 catch-up and revision, as far as the cohort needs (to confirm with each pupil's prior school).

units.title: Resource management: food, water and energy in the UK
points: Food, water and energy are fundamental to human development; global inequalities.
Changing demand and provision of food, water and energy in the UK.

units.title: Food (school option; water and energy options not taught)
points: Global food supply: surplus, deficit and food insecurity.
Strategies to increase food supply, with a large-scale agricultural example and an LIC or NEE local scheme.
Sustainable food supply.

commandWords.meaning: Say what something is like or set out its features.
Weigh up importance and reach a judgement.
Judge from evidence, weighing strengths and weaknesses.
Judge how far a statement is true, with evidence on both sides.

prerequisites.from: Year 8 weather, climate and climate change

links.how: Biology explains food webs and nutrient cycles; Geography applies them to biomes.
History explains why UK cities grew; Geography studies their change now.

contextNote: Teach the formation of the Earth's landscapes over geological time as the specification requires; where it fits, note that the Qur'an calls on people to reflect on the earth and mountains.
gaps: Changed 11 Nov 2026 from Pearson International GCSE 4GE1 to AQA GCSE 8035, because the school's booklet and Year 10 lessons use 8035 and its case studies (owner: the booklet wins).
Options follow the booklet: hot deserts (not cold environments); coasts and rivers (not glacial); food (not water or energy).
Fieldwork: AQA requires a Head of Centre statement. For online pupils sitting as private candidates, confirm a centre will accept the entry and sign it.
The full PDF was not read as raw text; check the key ideas against it before the first mock.
